questions.text: I find it energizing to direct a team through a challenging situation.
I have cried from the sheer intensity of a sunset, a piece of art, or an act of kindness.
I sense the unspoken ranking of whose time is considered most valuable in a professional setting.
When a coworker or neighbor is struggling, I feel little wish to help them.
I verify that backups of important data are running correctly on a regular basis.
I feel a deep sense of duty to use everything I have in service of others.
I notice that emotional content in conversations registers with me but doesn't alter my breathing or posture.
I write down lessons from each project so I can apply them to the next one.
I find it difficult to overrule suggestions, even when they do not align with my own thinking.
Feeling the weight of others' hardship keeps me from becoming complacent about it.
I lay out my clothes, pack my bag, or prepare materials the night before.
What some call procrastination, I experience as waiting for the right moment of clarity.
I rarely sense when a group has an unspoken agreement about who the designated leader is.
I often start projects without a clear plan, trusting that the path will reveal itself.
A stranger's visible distress makes me want to step in.
I am usually more aware of the logical flow of a conversation than its emotional currents.
I am the one who cuts off brainstorming to move the group into execution.
I keep working when I'm energized regardless of what my schedule says, and rest when the energy fades.
I feel a genuine pull to act when I encounter suffering, not just to notice it.
I believe that assembling a life that reflects my personal values and desires is the primary task of adulthood.
I am comfortable overruling a group decision when I believe I am right.
When I'm moved by something, the feeling washes over me like a wave.
I can receive bad news without my body going into alarm mode.
I notice when a person touches their face or neck during a conversation as a self-soothing gesture.
I intuitively understand the unspoken hierarchy in any social group I enter.
I let the group find its own course, even if I see a different path.
Knowing that a person is struggling seldom makes me want to do anything about it.
I find purpose in being the one who shoulders the burden so others don't have to.
I routinely rearrange my environment to maximize my own comfort and productivity.
When I see that someone is suffering, it usually makes no difference to what I want to do next.
When I feel at peace, the sensation is so vivid and complete that it's almost sacred.
I tend to be the last person to realize when a social event is winding down.
I notice that my emotional reactions rarely interfere with my ability to function.
I would give up a front-row seat so a stranger could have a better experience.
I tend to see networking as a way to build my own opportunities, first and foremost.
I prefer to ask questions that help someone see for themselves whether their approach is working.
